newsitem.title: USA: Former U.S. commander says scrap nuclear weapons.
newsitem.headline: Former U.S. commander says scrap nuclear weapons.

text.p: A former chief of U.S. Strategic Command who once oversaw part of America's nuclear arsenal spoke out on Thursday about why he now believes nuclear weapons should be abolished.

Former Air Force Gen. Lee Butler retired in 1994 after 37 years in uniform, reaching the position of commander in chief of the U.S. Strategic Command, where he was responsible for all Air Force and Navy strategic nuclear forces.
He was also involved in recasting the U.S. defence stance and shrinking its arsenals after the Cold War.

Speaking at the "State of the World Forum," an international conference here co-chaired by former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev, Butler said he is now convinced "that a world free of the threat of nuclear weapons is necessarily a world devoid of nuclear weapons."

Comparing the nuclear weapons arena to a large puzzle, Butler said he may be one of the few who had been able to look at all of the pieces from high-level policy-making to the people on missile silos, submarines and aircraft.

"When I got done and I put all the pieces together, I discovered that the puzzle didn't make any sense. The premise didn't make any sense and that is somehow we could find security in nuclear weapons," he told reporters.
"I think we were extraordinarly fortunate to escape the Cold War without a nuclear conflict," he said.

Butler was a member of the Canberra Commission on the Elimination of Nuclear Weapons, set up by the Australian government, which urged nuclear powers in August to cut their weapons stockpiles as a matter of urgency.

Butler, now in private business, said he had decided when he retired not to speak publicly on national security matters. He said he was speaking out now because he feared that the historic opportunities opened up by the end of the Cold War were slipping away.
"Options are being lost as urgent questions are marginalized," Butler said, pointing to the threat of nuclear proliferation.

However, he believed it was possible to forge a consensus that nuclear weapons have no defensible role and that the case for their elimination is "a thousand-fold stronger and more urgent than for deadly chemicals and viruses already widely declared illegitimate ..."

Butler urged the five declared nuclear states to accept that the Cold War is over and called on undeclared nuclear states "to embrace the harsh lessons of the Cold War" that nuclear weapons are hugely expensive, militarily inefficient and morally indefensible.
He said the United States should undertake a sweeping review of nuclear policies and strategies. "The nuclear beast must be chained, its soul expunged, its lair laid waste," he said.
